extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism/media studies; newsroom managers and working journalists interested in organizational production of news
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how news organizations classify events (spot, developing, continuing), allocate resources, and use professional routines and technology to convert everyday occurrences into routinized news. Focuses on temporal rhythms, prediction, and flexibility in newsroom work practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advance-prepared feature/seasonal stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual ‘February stories’ and similar items appropriate for holidays or anniversaries may be assigned days in advance and have specific information gathered, written, and edited before dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use advance assignment and pre-gathering to conserve personnel and control flow of work; these stories can be slotted into production schedules well before the event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling exceptions to advance preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature information about unscheduled events (e.g., atmosphere at an important trial or an unscheduled fire) cannot be gathered in advance, but news organizations handle such exceptions to conserve personnel and retain control of newswork.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign feature angles in advance where possible (striking reporter from fast-breaking roster), or have the same reporter cover both hard-news and soft-news angles to conserve staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot news (definition and processing urgency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spot-news events are unscheduled; they appear suddenly and must be processed quickly — the specifically unforeseen event-as-news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect rapid information gathering and editing; constraints like proximity to deadline and distance (transportation) affect speed and allocation of resources; plan for quick reallocation of staff when spot events occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stable social arrangements for anticipated but unschedulable spot events
rubrics_metrics.description: Some important yet low-probability spot-news events prompt newsworkers to create stable arrangements to anticipate them (e.g., 24-hour staffing to cover the president).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain extended allocations (overnight desks) and ability for immediate reallocation (pulling reporters from other stories) to cope if such an event occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology/time-rhythms influence on allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Different news technologies have varying time rhythms (film can be shot/edited/aired quickly; print is more time-consuming), and technology influences the organization of work and typifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design staffing and workflows according to medium: print requires more labor-intensive processes and reserve staff, television relies on faster turnarounds and different reserve patterns; be aware that technology shapes what is perceived as spot vs developing news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range of operational responses to unforeseen events (TV example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specifically unforeseen event occurs at non-peak times, a station may: pay overtime; pull reporter and cameraman from another story; pull a cameraman from a silent-film assignment; hire a freelance cameraman; pull a staff announcer; or assign a newswriter to act as reporter after union permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose alternative(s) based on the specific situation, especially the dispersion of crews and occurrences in time and space at that moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Developing news (emergent situations and evolving facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing news concerns emergent situations where initial accounts contain limited, reconstructable ‘facts’ that become more accurate as more information is known; ongoing changes are called ‘developing news.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that facts will be reconstructed and updated; structure copy and production to accommodate continual revision and amplification as new information arrives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology shapes perception of developing news
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology provides a lens through which events-as-news are perceived; different media may label the same event differently (TV vs print) depending on their technological rhythms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for how medium-specific rhythms (e.g., network bulletins vs local production constraints) affect editorial decisions, prominence, and update frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interchangeability of spot and developing news in practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Most spot-news stories are also developing news; staffs often use the terms interchangeably, though television may apply 'developing news' more restrictively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize overlap in categories when planning coverage and resource allocation; do not assume mutually exclusive handling procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production impact of developing news (layout and edition decisions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing news demands continual updates that can force repeated reformatting and relayout (e.g., multiple front-page resets after bulletins), affecting deadlines and production workload.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare production teams for repeated format changes; weigh choices like holding an edition versus releasing earlier copy, keeping in mind competition from faster media (television).

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing news (prescheduled series and predictability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing news is a series of stories on the same subject based upon events occurring over time (e.g., legislative bills); these events are prescheduled and imply prespecified change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reporters' cumulative stock of professional knowledge to predict trajectories and schedule coverage; continuing news facilitates control of work by enabling anticipation and routine processing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing news as organizational control
rubrics_metrics.description: Because continuing news is prescheduled, it helps newsworkers and organizations regulate activities by freeing staff to deal with unforeseen exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign beats and cultivate procedural knowledge so staff can predict and slot continuing items into the schedule, thereby enabling flexibility elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for continuing stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers seek continuing stories because they are predictably and readily covered and enable routine processing by prediction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance pursuit of predictable series with need to cover spot/developing stories; use continuing beats to stabilize staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typifications as a tool to routinize raw occurrences
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsworkers use typifications to transform idiosyncratic everyday occurrences into raw materials that can be subjected to routine processing and dissemination; typifications channel perceptions and impose a frame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and maintain classification schemes to reduce variability and enable routine responses, but be mindful of framing effects on what is considered newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectification and seduction of typifications (risk of error)
rubrics_metrics.description: If typifications become objectified (taken for granted), they can be seductive and lead to inaccurate predictions and errors in assessing newsworthiness (e.g., Wilson-Heath, Dewey-Truman examples).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate habitual typifications; remain open to reinterpreting events rather than over-relying on collective assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘What-a-story!’ typification for surprising events
rubrics_metrics.description: Inaccurately predicted or especially consequential events are handled via a special typification—‘What-a-story!’—constituted in unusual arrangements routinely invoked to cope with the event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have established emergency routines for processing major unexpected stories (rapid reallocation, invoking past precedents, special production arrangements); recognize the social/ritual aspects (verbal gestures) that accompany such invocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism as basis for flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Professionalism (exercise of autonomy, ‘professional instinct’) enables reporters to manage variability of raw materials and organizational flexibility; professionals control their work often via norms external to the organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage professional judgment and autonomy rather than heavy direct supervision to maintain flexibility and cost-effective staffing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification alone is insufficient; need procedural know-how
rubrics_metrics.description: Classifying events (e.g., as spot news) does not specify how information should be gathered; reporters also need knowledge of how to cover specific event types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate practical, beat-specific skills and routines (how to cover fires vs politics) so staff can execute coverage effectively when assigned outside their specialty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalist capability: specialties yield when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Specialties are ignored when necessary; everyone must be capable of doing everyone else’s work — 'each specialist must be a generalist, and vice versa.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train reporters to be versatile; expect role-swapping during high-demand periods to avoid gaps in the news net.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of sources and professional stock of knowledge-at-hand
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters' familiarity with processes, committee members, power distribution, and other beats constitutes a professional stock of knowledge used to predict outcomes and guide coverage of continuing and developing stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build institutional memory and source networks to improve prediction and routine coverage; this knowledge enables efficient allocation and anticipatory planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition with faster media affects editorial timing choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions such as whether to hold a mail edition to include a speech are complicated by competition with television, which may carry events first, making some decisions less consequential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor in cross-media competition when making edition-hold decisions; consider the likelihood of being scooped and the resource costs of holding versus sending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prearranged network provisions can reduce local workload
rubrics_metrics.description: At television, prearrangements (e.g., network preempting the first minutes of a late newscast) can mean less local readjustment compared to print, where repeated page resets create heavy work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage network/centralized supports and prearrangements where possible to reduce local production strain; understand differences in labor demands across media.
